args.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a licence that on the face of it looks genuine. The owner is not expected to verify with the RTO whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority. If the licence appears genuine and the driver is competent, the owner has satisfied the duty.
supporting.fact_alignment: The owner hired a driver who produced a licence with an endorsement to drive 'transport vehicle'. The court held the owner had taken reasonable care and was not expected to verify further details about whether the licence covered a 'heavy goods vehicle' specifically.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most directly applicable precedent on what constitutes adequate checking. It quotes Lehru with approval and sets the benchmark: visual inspection of a facially genuine licence + competence test = sufficient. The owner is not required to make enquiries with RTOs across the country.
supporting.quote: 'When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. The owner would then take the test of the driver. If he finds that the driver is competent to drive the vehicle, he will hire the driver.'

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured. The breach must be conscious and wilful on the part of the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle. The insurer proved the breach, but the court still held the insurer liable to third parties with recovery rights against the owner.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where the insurer proves a licence breach, the third-party claim is not defeated — the insurer pays first and recovers from the owner. The owner's failure to check does not let the insurer off the hook vis-à-vis the claimant.
supporting.quote: 'Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor.'

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, but the insurer must pay the third party first and then recover from the owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no licence at all. The owner failed to produce the driver's licence despite being represented by counsel. The tribunal held the owner breached the fundamental condition but still ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even in the strongest case against the owner (driver had zero licence, owner did not produce it), the insurer's defence does not defeat the claim — it only entitles the insurer to recover from the owner. The third party is always protected.
supporting.quote: 'It is held that the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle... but on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner.'

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver holds an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge required for a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third party first and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no badge/authorisation to drive a maxi cab (transport vehicle). The insurer proved the breach but was directed to pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that the 'pay and recover' principle applies even where the licence deficiency is clear. The insurer's defence is not defeated in the sense of being rejected — it is upheld — but the remedy is recovery from the owner, not refusal to pay the third party.
supporting.quote: 'The insurer and insured are bound by the conditions enumerated in the Policy and the insurer is not liable to the insured if there is violation of Policy conditions... but the insurer who is made statutorily liable to pay compensation to third parties... shall be entitled to recover from the insured.'

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement on their licence to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held a valid LMV licence but lacked an endorsement to drive a Mahindra Maxi Cab as a commercial vehicle. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Supreme Court judgment limits the scope of licence-based defences. Where the driver holds a licence for the class of vehicle, the absence of a commercial endorsement does not let the insurer avoid third-party liability. This narrows what counts as a 'licence defect' that can even trigger recovery rights.
supporting.quote: 'The insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained in the driving licence.'

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence on the date of the accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of its third-party liability. An expired-but-renewed licence is not the same as no licence at all.
supporting.fact_alignment: The drivers held valid licences that had expired before the accident and were renewed afterwards. The court held this was not a fundamental breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Distinguishes between types of licence defects. An expired licence (later renewed) is less serious than a fake licence or no licence. The owner who hires a driver with an apparently valid licence that later expires is in a stronger position than one who hires a driver with no licence at all.
supporting.quote: 'The drivers who had not got their licences renewed on the date of accident do not stand on the same footing as the persons who did not have any licence at all... Mere fact that the driver... had not got his driving licence renewed on the date of the accident and got it renewed subsequently would not amount to breach of condition of the policy.'

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: An insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party judgment even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision considering whether 'pay and recover' applies in all circumstances. Held that it does, regardless of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.
supporting.why_it_matters: Closes the argument that a contractual policy (with extra premium) might allow the insurer to escape liability entirely. The insurer must always pay the third party first, then recover from the insured.
supporting.quote: 'Even if there is any violation or breach of condition of a policy, the insurer has to discharge the initial burden of proving the grounds taken under Section 149(2) of the Act. In spite of that, the insurer has to indemnify the amount and can recover the same from the insured.'

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks and does not extend to own-damage claims. Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the client is the owner of the vehicle making an own-damage claim (e.g., for vehicle repair), the insurer can repudiate the claim entirely if the driver had a fake licence. The 'pay and recover' principle does not apply to own-damage claims. This is a complete defence for the insurer in non-third-party contexts.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case expressly limits its holding to own-damage/non-third-party claims. For third-party injury/death claims (which are the typical motor accident claim), Swaran Singh and the pay-and-recover line of authority continue to apply. The client's exposure depends on the nature of the claim.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: For driving a goods carriage carrying dangerous/hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving licence under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules is mandatory. The owner has a specific duty under Rule 132(5) to ensure the driver holds such an endorsement.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the vehicle was carrying hazardous goods (e.g., a tanker carrying oil/chemicals), the owner's duty is elevated beyond the general 'facially genuine licence' test. Rule 132(5) casts a specific statutory duty on the owner to verify the special endorsement. Failure to do so is a clear breach, and the insurer gets recovery rights.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This applies only where the vehicle is carrying 'dangerous or hazardous goods' as defined under the Rules. For ordinary goods vehicles or passenger vehicles, the general Lehru/Chennamma standard applies — the owner need only check that the licence appears genuine on its face.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
